title: Rook mate: the box
summary: King and rook against king: build the box, shrink it and mate on the edge.
part.box.title: The rook's box
part.box.summary: The rook builds the fence; the king protects it and pushes.
part.guard.title: Rook attacked: the king defends
part.guard.summary: So far the black king never reached the rook. When he does, it doesn't have to run.
part.far.title: Rook attacked, king far away
part.far.summary: What if your king is on the other side of the board? Count the moves of both kings.
part.run.title: The king that runs
part.run.summary: The rook isn't attacked, but the king is still far away: cut off first, run afterwards.
part.edge.title: On the edge: the next file
part.edge.summary: The king has reached the sixth. The next file, the check with opposition and the quiet move.
part.quiet.title: The waiting move
part.quiet.summary: In the previous part the black king still had somewhere to go. Here he has nothing, if he is forced to move.
part.stalemate.title: Stalemate and summary
part.stalemate.summary: You have learned to take squares away. The danger is taking them all.
step.t_box: The rook on h3 already stops the black king from coming down. How do you shrink that piece of the board without losing the rook?
step.t_box.hint1: A rook cuts off a rank and a file at the same time.
step.t_box.hint2: Next to your king, the rook is protected. Look there for the file closest to the black king.
step.box: You already gave this mate at school. The rook on h3 is a fence: the black king cannot come below the fourth rank. He lives inside a box, and the box is still huge. The whole job in this ending is one thing: shrink that box until it fits on the edge.
step.d_box: After Rc3, the black king went to b5. Now watch the box shrink all the way to mate. Every move, three questions, in this order: can the rook shrink the box safely? If not, the king steps up to help it. If not even that, the rook makes a waiting move.
step.d_box.m1: Kb3. The rook cannot shrink the box any further without being lost, so the king steps up, right next to it, and keeps defending c3.
step.d_box.m2: The black king goes up to b6. He cannot go down: a4 and b4 are now next to your king.
step.d_box.m3: Kb4. The king steps up again, still next to the rook. Now the fifth rank is his as well.
step.d_box.m4: The black king retreats to b7, away from your king, which now controls the fifth rank.
step.d_box.m5: Kb5. One more rank: a6 and b6 are now forbidden to the black king too.
step.d_box.m6: The black king goes to a7, away from your king, so as not to be pushed face to face.
step.d_box.m7: Kc6! The king stands a knight's jump from the black king and takes away b6 and b7. What is left is a6, a8 and b8, all on the edge.
step.d_box.m8: The black king goes to b8. On a6 it would be worse: Ra3 would mate at once.
step.d_box.m9: Kb6. The kings face to face. The c-file is still closed, so the black king only has a8.
step.d_box.m10: Ka8, the only square: c8 is on the rook's file, and a7 and b7 are next to your king.
step.d_box.m11: Rc8#. The rook goes up the c-file and closes the eighth rank; your king covers a7 and b7. The box has shrunk into the corner.
step.shrinkMove: White to move. Shrink the box with a rook move, without leaving the rook undefended within reach of the black king.
step.shrinkMove.hint: A rook closes a rank and a file at the same time. Look for a square that closes a file next to the black king and is protected by your king.
step.shrinkMove.done: That's it. With the rook on c3, the box became a corridor two files wide, from a4 to b8. And the rook stands next to your king, protected.
step.kingMove: White to move. The rook cannot shrink the box safely: on b4 the black king would take it. What is the second question?
step.kingMove.hint: The black king attacks b4. Bring your king closer so it can defend that square next move.
step.kingMove.done: Well done. With the king on c3, the rook goes to b4, defended, next move. Rc5+ also wins just as fast, but the simplest way is the king. Rook and king work together: one fences, the other protects.
step.t_guard: The black king attacks the rook on f4. Does it have to run?
step.t_guard.hint1: The rook is on a good square: it cuts off the f-file and the fourth rank.
step.t_guard.hint2: Who can protect f4 without the rook leaving it?
step.guard: The rook on f4 is on a great square: it holds the black king on the g- and h-files, from the fifth rank up. Running away with it, to f8, f3 or e4, keeps a fence, but your king stays far away and the mate gets two moves longer or more. Better to leave it there and bring the king to protect it: Kg3! defends f4 and steps up as well. Kf3 also defends, one move slower. Kh3? and Kf2? don't touch f4, and the rook falls.
step.d_guard: Watch the king protect the rook and then climb with it.
step.d_guard.m1: Kg3. The king defends f4 and is already closer to the black king.
step.d_guard.m2: The black king leaves the rook alone: defended, it cannot be taken.
step.d_guard.m3: Rg4. Now the rook shrinks the box, still defended by the king on g3. The black king only has the h-file.
step.d_guard.m4: The black king goes up to h7. He only has the h-file, and he prefers to stay away from your king.
step.d_guard.m5: Kf4. The king climbs the f-file, still next to the rook.
step.d_guard.m6: The black king goes to h8, as far as possible from your king.
step.d_guard.m7: Kf5. One more rank, and the rook on g4 stays protected.
step.d_guard.m8: Kh7, the only square: the g-file is closed.
step.d_guard.m9: Kf6. The rook no longer needs the king: the black king cannot leave the h-file and can never reach g4.
step.d_guard.m10: He goes back to h8. Black king on the edge and your king on the sixth: you will see the finish in the part about the edge.
step.glue: The rook can even stand right next to the black king, as long as your king defends it. Here the rook on g4 is attacked by the black king and defended by your king on f3. There is a square right next to him, also defended, that cuts off more.
step.glueMove: White to move. Shrink the box with the rook right next to the black king, but defended.
step.glueMove.hint: Look on the fourth rank for a square next to the black king that your king protects.
step.glueMove.done: Re4! Right next to the black king and defended by Kf3: the box now runs from f5 to h8.
step.t_far: The black king attacks the rook, and your king is on the other side of the board. Where does it go without leaving the sixth rank?
step.t_far.hint1: Far from the black king it is safe, but the box grows.
step.t_far.hint2: Count how many moves the black king needs to attack the new square, and how many your king needs to defend it.
step.far: Here the king cannot get there in time to defend a6: the rook has to leave. To where? It is a count. On e6, the black king needs two moves to attack it, Kc7 and Kd7, and your king also needs two to defend it, Kg5 and Kf6: it arrives in time. On d6, the rook is attacked at once by ...Kc7 and loses a tempo. On c6, it is lost. From h6 to f6 it is safe, but the black king gets more files.
step.d_far: Watch the count happen on the board.
step.d_far.m1: Re6. The square from the count: the closest one to the black king that your king can defend in time.
step.d_far.m2: The black king goes after the rook.
step.d_far.m3: Kg5. One move each: your king is coming too.
step.d_far.m4: Kd7. The black king arrives and attacks the rook on e6: now it is your king's turn to answer.
step.d_far.m5: Kf6. Just in time: the rook is defended, and the black king is still trapped on the a- to d-files, on the seventh and eighth ranks.
step.d_far.m6: The black king retreats to d8: the rook is defended, and there is nothing left for him to attack.
step.d_far.m7: Re7! Right next to the black king and defended by your king, the idea from the previous part. Now he only has the eighth rank.
step.farMove: White to move. The black king attacks the rook and your king is far away. Save the rook without leaving the third rank, and bring the king.
step.farMove.hint: The rook stays on the third rank. Count the moves of both kings to the new square.
step.farMove.done: That's it. ...Kf2 and ...Ke2 take two moves to attack d3, and so do Kb4 and Kc3: the rook is defended and the black king never got past the e-file.
step.t_run: Your king is on the other side of the board. Does it run right away, or does the rook do something first?
step.t_run.hint1: While your king travels, the black king moves too. How much room does he have?
step.t_run.hint2: The rook can trap him on the last rank right now, far from him.
step.run: First the cut: Rf7 traps the black king on the eighth rank, and on f7 the rook is far from him. Then the king runs along the diagonal, Kg5, Kf6 and Ke6, the shortest way. If the king runs first, the black king climbs to the middle and the mate takes four moves longer. Capablanca opens Chess Fundamentals this way: first the rook on the seventh, then the king comes along the diagonal.
step.d_run.m1: Rf7. The black king is trapped on the eighth, and the rook is far from him.
step.d_run.m2: The black king goes to d8, towards the rook.
step.d_run.m3: Kg5. Along the diagonal: the shortest way to the sixth rank, and towards the rook.
step.d_run.m4: Ke8. The black king attacks the rook on f7.
step.d_run.m5: Kf6. The king arrives just in time and protects the rook. The black king only has d8.
step.d_run.m6: Kd8, the only square: the seventh rank belongs to the rook, and f8 is on its file.
step.d_run.m7: Ke6. The king has reached the sixth rank, a knight's jump from the black king. From here on it is the mate on the edge, the next part.
step.runMove: White to move. Your king is far away. Trap the black king and bring your king to the sixth rank.
step.runMove.hint: First the rook: trap the black king on the last rank.
step.runMove.done: That's it. Cut off first, king along the diagonal afterwards: Rb7, Kb5 and Kc6, and your king has reached the sixth rank.
step.t_capablanca: The rook already holds the black king on the last rank. What is missing for mate, and how does your king get there?
step.t_capablanca.hint1: The black king can only move along the eighth rank. Where does your king take the most squares from him?
step.t_capablanca.hint2: Face to face, or on the next file? Think about where he goes back to.
step.capablanca: This is the position of Capablanca's first example in Chess Fundamentals, from 1921, after 5...Kc8. He plays Kd6!: on the sixth rank, the file next to the black king's, on the side of the centre. If the black king goes to d8, face to face, Ra8 is mate. Kc6? looks natural, but the black king goes back to d8 and the mate takes longer; the book itself warns about it.
step.d_capablanca: The moves from the book, from here on.
step.d_capablanca.m1: Kd6. On the next file, on the side of the centre. If ...Kd8, Ra8 is mate.
step.d_capablanca.m2: Kb8. The black king runs to the other side and attacks the rook.
step.d_capablanca.m3: Rc7! A quiet move, no check. The rook steps out of the attack and takes away c7 and c8: the black king only has a8.
step.d_capablanca.m4: Ka8, the only square: a7 and b7 are on the rook's rank, and c8 is on its file.
step.d_capablanca.m5: Kc6. The king follows along the sixth and protects the rook.
step.d_capablanca.m6: Kb8, again the only square: a7 and b7 are still on the rook's rank.
step.d_capablanca.m7: Kb6. Now the kings are face to face.
step.d_capablanca.m8: Ka8. The c-file is closed, so only the corner is left.
step.d_capablanca.m9: Rc8#. The rook closes the eighth rank, and your king on b6 covers a7 and b7. Mate, just as in the book.
step.opposition: When the rook alone can no longer shrink the box, the check comes in. But not just any check: the check that pushes is given when the kings stand face to face, one square apart. If the rook leaves the sixth rank to give check, your king on e5 still guards d6, e6 and f6. The black king has nowhere to go but back.
step.checkMove: White to move. The kings are in opposition. Push the black king back one rank.
step.checkMove.hint: With the kings face to face, a rook check on the black king's rank stops him from coming forward.
step.checkMove.done: Exactly. Ra7+ and the black king goes to the last rank. A check without opposition only chases the king; a check with opposition wins a rank.
step.quietMove: White to move and mate. No check on the first move.
step.quietMove.hint: Your king already covers d7 and e7. Which rook move covers the squares on the other side?
step.quietMove.done: Rc6! The black king only has e8, facing your king, and Rc8# closes the eighth rank. Rb8+? would let the black king out to c7, and the mate would be much further away.
step.t_iniyan: This position comes from a game between Nakamura, with White, and Iniyan, in a 2026 Titled Tuesday, a fast online tournament. Iniyan ran with his pawns against the rook; Nakamura took the last one on g3, and the black king went to g1. Rf1+ doesn't work: the king takes the rook. How do you mate?
step.t_iniyan.hint1: The black king has only one square. What if he is forced to move?
step.t_iniyan.hint2: The rook can move without leaving the f-file.
step.waiting: It is the waiting move. The rook moves along its own file, far from the black king, and the fence stays the same. But now he is the one who has to move, and all he has left is h1, a knight's jump from your king. Capablanca uses the same waiting move in the book's second example: the rook goes to any square on the file, and there the black king is forced to stand in front of the white one.
step.d_iniyan: This is how Nakamura finished the game.
step.d_iniyan.m1: Rf4. Waiting, far from the black king. Rf5 to Rf8, Rf2 and even Kh3 won just as fast; Rf1+ was the only move that spoiled it.
step.d_iniyan.m2: Kh1, the only square: f1 and f2 are on the rook's file, and g2 and h2 are next to the white king.
step.d_iniyan.m3: Rf1#. The king on g3 covers g2 and h2, and the rook closes the first rank. Mate, 1-0.
step.d_ahmad: The quiet move can also be a king move. Khagan Ahmad, with White, against Nakamura, in a 2025 Titled Tuesday: Nakamura gave his rook for the queen that had just been born on g8 and was left with a bare king. Thirteen moves later, his king is trapped on the a- to c-files, from the fourth rank up.
step.d_ahmad.m1: Kc5! The only move that mates fastest. No check: the king goes a knight's jump from the black king and takes away b4 and b5, leaving only a5.
step.d_ahmad.m2: Ka5. Nakamura has to stand face to face with the white king.
step.d_ahmad.m3: Ra3#. The rook checks along the a-file, and the white king covers b4, b5 and b6. Mate, 1-0.
step.waitMove: White to move and mate. Start with the waiting move and walk the black king into the corner.
step.waitMove.hint: The rook stays on the seventh rank, far from the black king. Your king walks along the sixth, always a knight's jump from the black king, until he has nowhere left to run.
step.waitMove.done: Mate. A waiting move, the king following closely, and the final check on the edge. It is the same picture you will repeat in every game.
step.kingQuiet: White to move and mate. The first move is a king move.
step.kingQuiet.hint: Leave the black king a single square, facing your king.
step.kingQuiet.done: Kf2! The black king only has h2, facing your king, and Rh4# closes the h-file.
step.t_stalemate: The black king is in the corner, with the rook and your king very close. Did White win, or let it slip? Count Black's moves.
step.t_stalemate.hint1: Is the black king in check? Where can it go?
step.stalemate: Now the danger. With the black king cornered, one move too many can take away all his moves without giving check. Here, with Black to move, the king on a8 has no legal move and is not in check: that is stalemate, a draw. Before every move near the corner, count the squares the black king still has. If it is zero without check, look for another move.
step.stalemateKing: Here it was the king that stalemated. The white king came to c8, facing the black king, and took away b7 and b8; the rook on the seventh covers a7. Black to move: no square and no check. A draw again. Near the corner, count the squares before every move, king or rook.
step.stalemateMove: White to move and win. Beware of the natural move.
step.stalemateMove.hint: Before moving the king, count the squares the black king will have. Zero squares without check is a draw.
step.stalemateMove.done: Kc2! gives him a2. Then Rd3, a quiet move, and Ra3# with your king a knight's jump away. Kc1?? would stalemate: the king on a1 would have no square at all.
step.recap: Three rules to take with you. One: cut off first and keep the rook safe, defended by the king or on a square the black king cannot reach before your king does. Two: the king climbs along the diagonal until it is a knight's jump from the black king; check only with the kings face to face. Three: without check, leave him a single square, with a waiting move or a quiet move, and near the corner count the squares before you move.
step.finish: Now the whole mate, from the centre. Build the box, shrink it, use the opposition and don't stalemate.
ex.e11: White to move and mate. The rook already closes the f-file; now your king has to do its part.
ex.e11.hint: Don't check yet. With your king, leave the black king a single square, and make that square a trap.
ex.e11.solution: Kg3! Your king takes g2 and h2, and the rook already covers f1 and f2: the black king only has h1. After ...Kh1, Rf1#. It is the corner mate, with your king a knight's jump away, but here it is your king that pushes the black king into the corner. Kf3 also wins, only the black king gets h2 and the mate takes longer.
ex.e12: White to move and mate. No check on the first move.
ex.e12.hint: Count the black king's squares. A quiet rook move can take all of them but one, and that one is right in front of your king.
ex.e12.solution: Rf7! The rook takes g7 and h7, and your king already covers g6 and g5: the black king only has h5, facing your king, and Rh7# closes the h-file. Rh8+? lets the black king out to g7, where he still attacks the rook, and Rg8 leaves h7 free: both win, but much more slowly.
ex.e13: White to move and win. The rook is attacked. Is running away the only way?
ex.e13.hint: The rook is on a great square: it cuts the d-file and the fifth rank. Ask yourself whether you can keep it there.
ex.e13.solution: Kc4! Your king defends the rook, which keeps the black king locked in the corner from e6 to h8, and gets closer too. Running with the rook along the fifth rank (Rg5, Ra5) or to d4 also wins, but costs two more moves: your king stays far away. After ...Kf6, Kc5 keeps going. Kc3?? or Kb4?? let the rook be taken.
ex.e14: White to move and mate. The move that looks natural only draws.
ex.e14.hint: Before bringing your king closer, count the squares the black king will have. Zero squares without check is a draw.
ex.e14.solution: Kg6! The black king only has g8. After ...Kg8, Rf1! (quiet, no check) leaves him only h8, and Rf8# closes the eighth rank with your king a knight's jump away. Kh6?? is stalemate: the king on h8 has no move and is not in check. Rg7?? and Rg8+?? give the rook away.
ex.e15: White to move and win. The black king attacks the rook, but it is defended. What is the strongest move?
ex.e15.hint: A rook can stand right next to the black king, as long as your king defends it. Look for the defended square that cuts the most.
ex.e15.solution: Re7! The rook is still defended by your king on f8 and now cuts the e-file: the black king is locked on the f, g and h files. After ...Kg6, Rf7! does the same again, also right next to him and defended, and the box is now just the g and h files. Running far away (Ra7, Rh7, Rg1) also wins, but the box gets much bigger.
ex.e16: White to move and mate by the shortest road. Your king is on the other side of the board.
ex.e16.hint: First lock the black king on the last rank. Then your king travels: the diagonal is the shortest road, and it must reach the sixth rank facing the black king or a knight's jump from him.
ex.e16.solution: Rh7! The black king is locked on the eighth rank and only has b8. Now the white king runs along the diagonal: Kg4, Kf5, Ke6, and walks along the sixth rank next to the black king, Kd6 and Kc6. When he reaches a8, Kb6 leaves him only b8, facing your king, and Rh8#. Kg4 on the first move also wins, but the black king gets out through the seventh rank and everything takes longer.
ex.e17: White to move and win. The rook is attacked and your king is far away. Where does it go?
ex.e17.hint: The rook must keep cutting the f-file, far from the black king, on a square your king can defend before the black king gets there. Count the moves of both kings.
ex.e17.solution: Rf4! The black king needs two moves to attack it (Kg6 and Kg5), and your king also needs two to defend it (Ke2 and Kf3). It is the square closest to the black king where this works. Rf5? shrinks the box more, but ...Kg6 attacks it again and you lose a move; Rf3, Rf2 and Rf1 are safe, but the box is bigger. After ...Kh7, Ke2 and Kf3: the rook is defended and the box is about to shrink.
key.box: The box: the rook cuts a rank, or a rank and a file, and the black king is trapped in a rectangle. The plan is to shrink the rectangle down to the edge.
key.edgeMate: The basic mate: the black king on the edge, the white king facing him, and the rook checks along the edge. A classic diagram, as in Wikipedia.
key.cornerMate: The corner mate: the kings are not face to face, the white king stands a knight's jump away and the rook closes the a-file.
key.stalemate: The most common stalemate of this ending: rook on b7 defended by the king, Black has no move and no check. A draw.
key.capablanca: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals, 1921, the first example of the book: with the black king on the last rank, Kd6!, on the file next to the black king's, and not Kc6.
history: Capablanca opened his Chess Fundamentals, in 1921, with this mate. For him it was how a beginner gets to know the power of the pieces: drive the enemy king to the edge, keep your own king on the same rank or file as his and, once on the sixth, stand on the file next to it, on the side of the centre. He admitted the exercise is monotonous, but said it is worth it: it teaches you to handle the pieces. Today people talk about a box: the rook closes a rectangle and every move makes it smaller. Lichess teaches this mate in its piece checkmates practice, and there are community studies just on the box method. The ending turns up even among the best players in the world: in a 2026 chess.com Titled Tuesday, Nakamura took Iniyan's last pawn and mated with a rook waiting move (61.Rf4 Kh1 62.Rf1#); in a 2025 one, Khagan Ahmad mated Nakamura with a quiet king move (94.Kc5 Ka5 95.Ra3#). Both games are in PGN Mentor's public archive of Nakamura's games. With the rook and the move, the mate always comes: just don't stalemate and don't let the rook be taken.
practice: Now the real ending: king and rook against the black king in the centre. Build the box, shrink it, use the opposition and don't stalemate. Pick your time control and go.
